subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look around you. Whether you live near the busy streets of Mogadishu, the green hills of Hargeisa, the coast of Mombasa, or a village beside the Jubba River, you are surrounded by living things. The acacia tree bending in the wind, the goats nibbling dry grass, the tilapia swimming in a river, the tiny ants marching across the ground, and even the bacteria you cannot see in the soil are all part of one enormous, connected story. In this unit you will learn how all these living things depend on one another and on the non-living world around them.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Science 0846 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Explain what an ecosystem and a habitat are, and describe the biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) factors within them.
Describe how plants act as producers and capture energy from the sun through photosynthesis.
Classify animals as primary, secondary, and tertiary consumers, and as herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores.
Explain the vital role of decomposers in recycling nutrients back into the soil.
Build and read food chains and food webs, using arrows correctly to show the flow of energy.
Explain why energy decreases at each step of a food chain and why there are fewer top predators than plants.
Describe how living things show adaptations that help them survive in their habitat.
Evaluate how human activities such as deforestation, overfishing, drought, and plastic pollution affect ecosystems.
Suggest conservation actions that protect living things, connecting this to the responsibility of caring for the Earth.

concepts.title: Ecosystems and Habitats
concepts.explanation:
An ecosystem is made up of two kinds of things working together: the living things, called biotic factors, and the non-living things, called abiotic factors. Imagine the savanna near Garissa early in the morning. The grass, the acacia trees, the gazelles, the lions, the birds, and the tiny insects are all biotic — they are alive. The sunshine warming the ground, the temperature of the air, the water in a nearby waterhole, the soil beneath your feet, and the wind moving the grass are all abiotic — they are not alive, but living things could not survive without them.

A habitat is the specific home where an organism lives and finds everything it needs: food, water, shelter, and a safe place to raise its young. The savanna is the habitat of the gazelle. The Indian Ocean coral reef is the habitat of the parrotfish. A patch of moist soil is the habitat of an earthworm. Different organisms need different habitats because they need different things. A camel is well suited to hot, dry, semi-arid land, but a tilapia would die there in minutes because it needs water. A mangrove crab thrives where salty seawater meets the land, but it could not survive on a dry mountain.

Every habitat must supply four basic needs: food, water, shelter, and space. When one of these is missing or runs short — for example, when a long drought dries up the waterholes — animals must move, adapt, or they may not survive. This is why the same ecosystem can look full of life in the wet season and much quieter in the dry season.

Did You Know? A single teaspoon of healthy soil can contain more living microorganisms than there are people on the whole Earth. The mangrove forests along the East African coast are nurseries where baby fish hide and grow before swimming out to the open ocean.

Living things are shaped by their habitat through adaptation. An adaptation is a special feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive where it lives. The camel is a champion of adaptation to dry, semi-arid land: it stores fat in its hump for energy, can go many days without drinking, has long eyelashes to keep out blowing sand, and wide feet that do not sink into loose ground. The acacia tree has long roots that reach deep for water and sharp thorns that protect its leaves from hungry animals. A gazelle has long legs for fast running to escape lions, and eyes on the sides of its head to watch for danger in every direction. Each adaptation is a clue to the habitat the animal or plant calls home.

Ecosystems come in many types, and East Africa is rich with them. The dry, grassy savanna is home to lions, gazelles, zebras, and giraffes. The semi-arid scrubland, where herders graze their camels and goats, has tough thorny plants that survive with little rain. Along the shore, warm coral reefs shelter thousands of colourful fish, while mangrove forests, where salty seawater meets the land, protect the coast and shelter young fish. Inland, the Rift Valley lakes draw great flocks of flamingos. Each of these ecosystems has its own balance of biotic and abiotic factors, and its own community of living things that fit it perfectly. When you learn to read an ecosystem, you begin to see why each animal lives exactly where it does.

It helps to think of an ecosystem as a large, busy household in which every member has a role, and the non-living surroundings — the walls, the water supply, the warmth — make daily life possible. Change one part of the household and everyone feels it. If the water supply fails, or the temperature soars, the whole community must respond. This is why scientists never study a single animal alone; they study the animal together with everything around it. Throughout this unit, keep asking two questions about any living thing you meet: 'What does it need from its habitat?' and 'What would happen to the others if it disappeared?'

Think about these questions and discuss them with your AI tutor. There is no need to rush — reasoning them out slowly is the point.

Why can a camel survive in dry semi-arid land while a fish cannot? List the abiotic factors that make the difference.

Name three biotic and three abiotic factors in a mangrove ecosystem along the coast near Kismaayo.
concepts.example: During a long drought, what might happen to the animals in a savanna habitat? Where might they go?

concepts.title: Producers: The Foundation of All Life
concepts.explanation:
Every food chain begins with a producer. A producer is a living thing that can make its own food. Green plants are the most common producers on land. They do something amazing that no animal can do: they capture the energy of sunlight and use it to make sugar, a kind of food, inside their leaves. This process is called photosynthesis. The word means 'putting together with light'. During photosynthesis a plant takes in sunlight, water from the soil through its roots, and carbon dioxide gas from the air, and it makes sugar for energy while giving out the oxygen that we breathe.

Because producers make their own food, they do not need to eat other living things. Instead, they trap the sun's energy and store it. This stored energy is the starting point for almost every other living thing on Earth. When a gazelle eats grass, it is really taking in energy that first came from the sun and was captured by the grass. When a lion eats the gazelle, that same sun-energy passes on again. This is why we say producers are the foundation of all life — without them, there would be no energy entering the ecosystem at all.

Producers are everywhere. On the savanna, the grasses and acacia trees are the main producers. In a farm near the Jubba River, the maize, banana, and mango plants are producers. In the Indian Ocean, tiny floating plants and plant-like living things called plankton and algae are the producers — they are so small you often need a microscope to see them, yet they feed the entire ocean and produce a large share of the world's oxygen.

It is worth pausing to picture photosynthesis clearly, because it is one of the most important processes on Earth. Inside every green leaf are countless tiny parts that hold a green colouring called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is what makes leaves green, and it acts like a trap for sunlight. When sunlight lands on the leaf, the chlorophyll catches its energy. The plant then uses that energy to join together the water it drew up from the soil and the carbon dioxide it took from the air, building them into sugar — the plant's food. As a by-product, the plant releases oxygen into the air. So every breath of clean air you take is a gift from producers busy at work. When you sit under the shade of a mango or baobab tree, remember that its leaves are quietly turning sunlight into food and filling the air with oxygen at the same time.

Because producers turn sunlight into stored food energy, scientists call the amount of food they make the primary production of an ecosystem. Where there is plenty of sunlight, water, and rich soil — such as a well-watered farm or a healthy mangrove — primary production is high and the ecosystem can feed many consumers. Where conditions are harsh — such as bare, dry, semi-arid land during a drought — primary production is low, and far fewer animals can be supported. This simple idea explains why the green savanna after the rains bursts with life, while the same land in a long dry season falls quiet.
concepts.example: [*] Remember! Producers make their own food using sunlight. Consumers cannot — they must eat. The energy in every food chain starts as sunlight captured by a producer. No producers means no food and no energy for anything else in the ecosystem.

concepts.title: Consumers and Feeding Relationships
concepts.explanation:
A consumer is a living thing that cannot make its own food, so it must eat other living things to get energy. You are a consumer. So is a gazelle, a lion, a tilapia, a chicken, and a mosquito. Scientists sort consumers into groups in two useful ways: by what they eat, and by where they sit in the food chain.

Sorting by what they eat gives us three groups. A herbivore eats only plants — the gazelle, the goat, the cow, and the camel are herbivores. A carnivore eats only other animals — the lion, the hyena, and the fish-eating heron are carnivores. An omnivore eats both plants and animals — human beings are omnivores, and so are chickens and baboons. Each type has adaptations for its diet: herbivores often have wide flat teeth for grinding grass, while carnivores have sharp pointed teeth for tearing meat.

Sorting by position in the food chain gives us levels called trophic levels. A primary consumer eats producers directly — it is a plant-eater, like the gazelle eating grass. A secondary consumer eats primary consumers — like a snake eating a mouse, or a small fish eating tiny water animals. A tertiary consumer eats secondary consumers — like a lion or a large Nile perch at the top of its chain. The animals at the very top, which nothing else hunts, are called top predators.

Here is a savanna example to hold in your mind. The grass is the producer. A gazelle eats the grass, so the gazelle is a primary consumer. A lion eats the gazelle, so the lion is a secondary consumer. In the ocean, tiny plankton are producers, a small tilapia eats the plankton as a primary consumer, and a larger fish such as a Nile perch eats the tilapia as a secondary consumer. Notice how the same idea works on land and in water.

Consumers depend completely on producers, even the fierce meat-eaters that never touch a plant. Think about it: a lion eats a gazelle, but the gazelle only had energy in its body because it had eaten grass. So the lion's meal is really sun-energy that passed first into the grass and then into the gazelle. This is why we say all consumers depend on producers — the energy in their food always traces back to sunlight captured by a plant. If the grass failed, the gazelles would starve, and then the lions would have nothing to hunt. Every consumer, however powerful, sits on top of the quiet work of producers.

Consumers also help control one another's numbers, keeping the ecosystem in balance. Predators such as lions and hyenas keep the numbers of grass-eaters in check, so the grass is not completely eaten away. In turn, the amount of grass available limits how many gazelles can live in an area. This gentle push and pull between predators and their prey keeps populations from growing too large or crashing too low. When you watch animals near your home, you are watching this balance in action, even if it is not obvious at first glance.

Did You Know? A lion may need to eat many gazelles across a year, which is why a large area of savanna can support only a few lions. Flamingos on East Africa's Rift Valley lakes are pink because of the tiny algae and shrimp they eat.

Classify each of these as herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore: goat, lion, human, heron, camel.

In the chain grass to gazelle to lion, name the producer, the primary consumer, and the secondary consumer.
concepts.example: Why do you think carnivores have sharp teeth while herbivores have flat teeth? Connect the answer to their food.

concepts.title: Decomposers: Nature's Recyclers
concepts.explanation:
When a plant dies, or an animal dies, or an animal leaves droppings, what happens to all that material? It does not simply pile up forever. A special group of living things gets to work: the decomposers. Decomposers are living things that break down dead plants, dead animals, and waste, returning the nutrients locked inside them back into the soil. The main decomposers are bacteria and fungi, but small animals such as earthworms and dung beetles also help.

Think of decomposers as nature's recyclers. When a fallen acacia leaf lies on the savanna floor, fungi and bacteria slowly break it apart. The valuable nutrients inside — the very minerals a plant needs to grow — are released into the soil. Then the roots of new grass and trees take up those nutrients, and grow strong, and become food for gazelles again. This never-ending loop is called the nutrient cycle. Nutrients are used again and again, passed from soil to plant to animal and back to soil.

Decomposers are easy to forget because much of their work happens hidden in the soil, out of sight. But they are absolutely essential. Imagine if there were no decomposers at all. Dead leaves, dead animals, and waste would build up and never break down. Worse, the nutrients trapped inside them would be lost forever, the soil would become poor, and eventually the producers could not grow. Without decomposers, the whole ecosystem would slowly starve. This is why a farmer who makes compost — a rich material made by letting fruit peels, leaves, and food scraps decompose — is really putting decomposers to work to feed the next crop.

Decomposers work best in warm, moist conditions, which is why food left out in warm weather spoils quickly, while food kept cool and dry lasts far longer. This same knowledge helps families in practical ways. Drying meat and fish in the sun, or keeping grain dry, are old and clever ways of slowing decomposers down so that food is not spoiled before it can be eaten. On the other hand, a farmer who wants to make good compost does the opposite: keeping the heap moist and warm so decomposers work faster and turn scraps into rich soil sooner. Understanding decomposers, then, is not only about science lessons — it helps you store food safely and grow healthier crops at home.
concepts.example: [*] Remember! Decomposers return nutrients from dead things back into the soil. The nutrient cycle moves nutrients: soil to producer to consumer and back to soil. Without decomposers, nutrients would be locked away and producers could not grow.

concepts.title: Food Chains, Food Webs, and the Flow of Energy
concepts.explanation:
A food chain is a simple way to show how energy passes from one living thing to the next. We draw it with arrows, and here is the most important rule to remember: the arrow always points in the direction the energy flows — that is, from the thing being eaten to the thing that eats it. So we write grass -> gazelle -> lion. The arrow from grass to gazelle means 'energy flows from the grass into the gazelle because the gazelle eats the grass'. A common mistake is to point the arrow the wrong way, toward the food. Always follow the energy, not the mouth.

In the real world, living things rarely eat just one thing, and they are rarely eaten by just one thing. A gazelle is hunted by lions, hyenas, and leopards. A lion eats gazelles, zebras, and buffalo. When we join many food chains together, we get a food web — a network that shows all the feeding relationships in an ecosystem at once. A food web is a truer picture of nature than a single chain, because it shows how many living things are connected.

Food webs teach us a powerful lesson: everything is connected. If one part changes, the whole web feels it. Suppose hunters removed all the lions from a savanna. With no lions to hunt them, the gazelle population might grow very large. Too many gazelles would eat too much grass, and the grass could be stripped bare. Then, with little grass left, many gazelles would starve, and other grass-eating animals would suffer too. Removing just one species can shake the entire system. This is why protecting each species matters.

Now, an important idea about energy. Energy enters the ecosystem as sunlight and is captured by producers. As it flows up the chain, something happens at every step: most of the energy is lost, mainly as heat and through the daily living, moving, and breathing of each animal. Only about one tenth — roughly ten percent — of the energy at one level passes on to the next level. The rest is used up staying alive.

This 'energy tax' at every step explains two things you can see in nature. First, it explains why food chains are usually short, with only four or five levels — after a few steps, there is simply not enough energy left to support another level of hunters. Second, it explains why there are always fewer animals at the top. A savanna has vast amounts of grass, many gazelles, but only a few lions. There is plenty of energy at the bottom of the chain and very little at the top. This pattern is sometimes drawn as a pyramid, wide at the producer base and narrow at the top predator tip.

Did You Know? Only about ten percent of the energy at one level of a food chain passes to the next level — the other ninety percent is used up living and moving. This is exactly why an ecosystem can feed thousands of grass plants, hundreds of gazelles, but only a handful of lions.

Let us work through the energy idea with numbers, step by step. Suppose the grass in one area captures 10,000 units of energy from the sun. Only about ten percent passes to the next level each time.

The grass (producer) holds 10,000 units of energy.

The gazelle (primary consumer) eats grass and receives about ten percent of 10,000, which is 1,000 units.

The lion (secondary consumer) eats the gazelle and receives about ten percent of 1,000, which is 100 units.

If a bigger predator ate the lion, it would receive only about 10 units — very little energy indeed.
concepts.example: Notice how quickly the energy shrinks: 10,000, then 1,000, then 100, then 10. After only a few steps there is almost nothing left. This is the clearest way to understand why food chains are short and why top predators must be few in number. When your AI tutor gives you a starting energy amount, you can find each level by taking ten percent — that is, dividing by ten — each time you move up the chain.

concepts.title: Human Impact and Caring for the Earth
concepts.explanation:
Human beings are part of ecosystems too, and our actions can help or harm them. Sadly, many human activities damage the natural world, and East Africa faces several of these challenges directly. Understanding the problems is the first step to solving them.

Deforestation means cutting down forests and trees, often for firewood, charcoal, or to clear land for farming. Trees are producers and homes; when they are removed, the animals that lived among them lose their habitat, the soil is no longer held by roots and washes away, and less rain may fall. Overfishing happens when people catch fish faster than the fish can breed and replace themselves. Along the Indian Ocean coast, taking too many fish can cause fish populations to collapse, hurting both the ocean food web and the families who depend on fishing for food and income.

Plastic pollution is a growing danger, especially on beaches and in the ocean. Plastic bags and bottles dropped on the sand are washed into the sea, where turtles may swallow them thinking they are jellyfish, and fish become tangled. Plastic does not decompose for hundreds of years. Drought, made worse by a changing climate, dries up waterholes and rivers, kills crops and grass, and forces both wild animals and herders with their camels and goats to travel far in search of water. Each of these problems ripples through the food web, harming many species at once.

But there is very good news: people can also protect and repair ecosystems. This work is called conservation. Conservation includes replanting trees to bring back forests, setting up protected areas where wildlife is safe, fishing in careful limits so fish stocks recover, cleaning plastic from beaches, and saving water during dry seasons. Every one of us can take part — planting a tree, avoiding littering, saving water, and telling others why nature matters.

For a Muslim, caring for the Earth is part of faith. The Qur'an describes people as khalifah, meaning stewards or caretakers entrusted with looking after the world. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught kindness to animals and even encouraged the planting of trees. So when you protect a habitat, save water, or care for an animal, you are doing something both scientific and good. Observing creation closely, with wonder and care, is one of the beautiful ways to reflect on the One who made it all.

Did You Know? A single mature tree can give a home to hundreds of insects, birds, and small animals, which is why replanting forests helps so many species at once. Sea turtles along the East African coast can mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish, which is one reason keeping beaches clean saves lives.
concepts.example: [*] Remember — You Are a Khalifah! Human actions like deforestation, overfishing, and pollution can damage whole food webs. Conservation means protecting and repairing nature: plant trees, save water, keep beaches clean. Caring for the Earth is a responsibility we all share.

methods.title: The Race to Rot: Decomposition Investigation
methods.example: To find out how decomposers break down different materials, and which materials rot and which do not.
steps: Place a little soil in each jar, or dig small shallow holes in the ground.
Bury one item in each jar or hole: fruit peel, leaf, bread, and plastic. Label each one.
Sprinkle a little water on each to keep the soil slightly moist, like after light rain.
Put the jars in a warm, shaded place. Keep the soil slightly damp through the week.
Every two or three days, gently uncover each item, observe it, then cover it again.

methods.title: Do Producers Need Light? The Covered Leaf Test
methods.example: To find out whether a green plant needs sunlight to stay healthy and make its food.
steps: Choose two healthy leaves of similar size on the same plant.
Cover one leaf completely with card or foil so no light reaches it. Leave the other leaf uncovered as your control.
Make sure the plant still gets water and sunlight as normal.
Wait for five to seven days.
Uncover the covered leaf and compare it with the uncovered one.

methods.title: A Mini-Ecosystem in a Bottle
methods.example: To build a small closed ecosystem and observe how living and non-living parts work together over time.
steps: With an adult's help, cut the top off the bottle if needed to place soil and the plant inside, or use a wide-mouth bottle.
Add a layer of soil about three fingers deep.
Plant the small plant or sprinkle grass seeds, and press the soil gently.
Add a small amount of water — just enough to make the soil moist, not flooded.
Seal the bottle with its lid or tape the top back on to close it.

methods.title: Counting Life: A Backyard Biodiversity Survey
methods.example: To measure the biodiversity — the variety of living things — in two different areas near your home.
steps: Choose two areas: one open and dry, one shaded under a tree, bush, or beside water.
Place your square frame on the ground in the first area.
Look carefully inside the square. Count how many different kinds of living things you can find: plants, insects, spiders, worms, birds passing, and so on.
Record each different kind and how many you see.
Repeat in the second area with the same size square.

workedExamples.title: Following the Energy
workedExamples.prompt: Let us work through the energy idea with numbers, step by step. Suppose the grass in one area captures 10,000 units of energy from the sun. Only about ten percent passes to the next level each time.
workedExamples.solution:
The grass (producer) holds 10,000 units of energy.

The gazelle (primary consumer) eats grass and receives about ten percent of 10,000, which is 1,000 units.

The lion (secondary consumer) eats the gazelle and receives about ten percent of 1,000, which is 100 units.

If a bigger predator ate the lion, it would receive only about 10 units — very little energy indeed.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: In a food chain, the arrow points: (a) from the eater to the food (b) from the food to the eater (c) in both directions (d) it does not matter.
workedExamples.solution: (b) from the food to the eater. The arrow shows the direction energy flows, into the animal that eats.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a producer? (a) gazelle (b) lion (c) acacia grass (d) earthworm.
workedExamples.solution: (c) acacia grass. Grass is a producer because it makes its own food by photosynthesis; the others must eat.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: An animal that eats only plants is called a: (a) carnivore (b) herbivore (c) omnivore (d) decomposer.
workedExamples.solution: (b) herbivore. A herbivore eats only plants, like a goat or gazelle.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which organism is a decomposer? (a) grass (b) fungus (c) gazelle (d) heron.
workedExamples.solution: (b) fungus. Fungi break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil, so they are decomposers.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: About how much energy passes from one level of a food chain to the next? (a) 100 percent (b) 50 percent (c) 10 percent (d) 0 percent.
workedExamples.solution: (c) 10 percent. About ninety percent is lost as heat and through living and moving, so only about ten percent passes on.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: In the chain plankton to tilapia to Nile perch, the tilapia is the: (a) producer (b) primary consumer (c) secondary consumer (d) decomposer.
workedExamples.solution: (b) primary consumer. The tilapia eats the producer (plankton) directly, so it is a primary consumer.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: A non-living part of an ecosystem, such as sunlight or water, is called a: (a) biotic factor (b) abiotic factor (c) consumer (d) producer.
workedExamples.solution: (b) abiotic factor. Abiotic means non-living, such as sunlight, water, soil, and temperature.

practice.prompt: In a food chain, the arrow points: (a) from the eater to the food (b) from the food to the eater (c) in both directions (d) it does not matter.
practice.answer: (b) from the food to the eater. The arrow shows the direction energy flows, into the animal that eats.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a producer? (a) gazelle (b) lion (c) acacia grass (d) earthworm.
practice.answer: (c) acacia grass. Grass is a producer because it makes its own food by photosynthesis; the others must eat.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: An animal that eats only plants is called a: (a) carnivore (b) herbivore (c) omnivore (d) decomposer.
practice.answer: (b) herbivore. A herbivore eats only plants, like a goat or gazelle.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Which organism is a decomposer? (a) grass (b) fungus (c) gazelle (d) heron.
practice.answer: (b) fungus. Fungi break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil, so they are decomposers.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: About how much energy passes from one level of a food chain to the next? (a) 100 percent (b) 50 percent (c) 10 percent (d) 0 percent.
practice.answer: (c) 10 percent. About ninety percent is lost as heat and through living and moving, so only about ten percent passes on.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: In the chain plankton to tilapia to Nile perch, the tilapia is the: (a) producer (b) primary consumer (c) secondary consumer (d) decomposer.
practice.answer: (b) primary consumer. The tilapia eats the producer (plankton) directly, so it is a primary consumer.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: A non-living part of an ecosystem, such as sunlight or water, is called a: (a) biotic factor (b) abiotic factor (c) consumer (d) producer.
practice.answer: (b) abiotic factor. Abiotic means non-living, such as sunlight, water, soil, and temperature.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Why are there usually fewer lions than gazelles in a savanna? (a) lions are lazy (b) energy decreases up the chain (c) gazelles eat lions (d) lions do not need food.
practice.answer: (b) energy decreases up the chain. With little energy left at the top, only a few lions can be supported.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Which human activity harms ocean food webs by taking too many fish? (a) conservation (b) photosynthesis (c) overfishing (d) composting.
practice.answer: (c) overfishing. Catching fish faster than they can breed collapses fish populations and the ocean food web.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: The camel's hump, storing fat for the dry season, is an example of a: (a) food chain (b) decomposer (c) adaptation (d) producer.
practice.answer: (c) adaptation. Storing fat in the hump is a feature that helps the camel survive dry seasons.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: What would most likely happen if all decomposers disappeared? (a) nutrients would return to the soil faster (b) dead matter would pile up and soil would grow poor (c) plants would grow better (d) nothing would change.
practice.answer: (b) dead matter would pile up and the soil would grow poor. Nutrients would stay locked in dead things, so producers could not grow.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

practice.prompt: Which is the correct order of a food chain? (a) lion to gazelle to grass (b) grass to gazelle to lion (c) gazelle to grass to lion (d) lion to grass to gazelle.
practice.answer: (b) grass to gazelle to lion. Energy flows from the producer, to the plant-eater, to the meat-eater.
practice.hint: Look back at what Ecosystem and Habitat mean in this unit, then answer in a full sentence.

activities.title: The Race to Rot: Decomposition Investigation
activities.materials: Three or four small clear jars or cups, or three shallow holes in garden soil; A small piece of fruit peel (banana or mango); A green leaf; A small piece of bread; A small piece of plastic (bottle cap or bag); Some soil, a little water, and a notebook
steps: Place a little soil in each jar, or dig small shallow holes in the ground.
Bury one item in each jar or hole: fruit peel, leaf, bread, and plastic. Label each one.
Sprinkle a little water on each to keep the soil slightly moist, like after light rain.
Put the jars in a warm, shaded place. Keep the soil slightly damp through the week.
Every two or three days, gently uncover each item, observe it, then cover it again.

activities.title: Do Producers Need Light? The Covered Leaf Test
activities.materials: A healthy potted plant, or a plant growing in the ground (a herb, bean, or any leafy plant); A piece of card, foil, or dark paper; A paper clip, tape, or string to hold it; A notebook
steps: Choose two healthy leaves of similar size on the same plant.
Cover one leaf completely with card or foil so no light reaches it. Leave the other leaf uncovered as your control.
Make sure the plant still gets water and sunlight as normal.
Wait for five to seven days.
Uncover the covered leaf and compare it with the uncovered one.

activities.title: A Mini-Ecosystem in a Bottle
activities.materials: A large clear plastic bottle with a lid (a used water or soda bottle, cleaned); Some soil; A tiny plant or a few grass seeds, or a small seedling; A little water; A sunny windowsill and a notebook
steps: With an adult's help, cut the top off the bottle if needed to place soil and the plant inside, or use a wide-mouth bottle.
Add a layer of soil about three fingers deep.
Plant the small plant or sprinkle grass seeds, and press the soil gently.
Add a small amount of water — just enough to make the soil moist, not flooded.
Seal the bottle with its lid or tape the top back on to close it.

activities.title: Counting Life: A Backyard Biodiversity Survey
activities.materials: A notebook and pencil; A simple frame such as a bent wire or a square drawn with string (about one big step on each side); Optional: a magnifying glass
steps: Choose two areas: one open and dry, one shaded under a tree, bush, or beside water.
Place your square frame on the ground in the first area.
Look carefully inside the square. Count how many different kinds of living things you can find: plants, insects, spiders, worms, birds passing, and so on.
Record each different kind and how many you see.
Repeat in the second area with the same size square.

activities.title: Observe: Food Chains, Food Webs, and the Flow of Energy
activities.materials: Three or four small clear jars or cups, or three shallow holes in garden soil; A small piece of fruit peel (banana or mango); A green leaf; A small piece of bread; A small piece of plastic (bottle cap or bag); Some soil, a little water, and a notebook
steps: Look for an example of food chains, food webs, and the flow of energy around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Ecosystem and Habitat.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

activities.title: Sort: Human Impact and Caring for the Earth
activities.materials: A healthy potted plant, or a plant growing in the ground (a herb, bean, or any leafy plant); A piece of card, foil, or dark paper; A paper clip, tape, or string to hold it; A notebook
steps: Look for an example of human impact and caring for the earth around your home or outside.
Find examples at home and sort them into groups, then explain your rule.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Ecosystem and Habitat.

rules.title: Ecosystems and Habitats
rules.text: An ecosystem is made up of two kinds of things working together: the living things, called biotic factors, and the non-living things, called abiotic factors.

rules.title: Producers: The Foundation of All Life
rules.text: Every food chain begins with a producer.

rules.title: Consumers and Feeding Relationships
rules.text: A consumer is a living thing that cannot make its own food, so it must eat other living things to get energy.

rules.title: Decomposers: Nature's Recyclers
rules.text: When a plant dies, or an animal dies, or an animal leaves droppings, what happens to all that material?

rules.title: Food Chains, Food Webs, and the Flow of Energy
rules.text: A food chain is a simple way to show how energy passes from one living thing to the next.

rules.title: Human Impact and Caring for the Earth
rules.text: Human beings are part of ecosystems too, and our actions can help or harm them.

terms: Ecosystem
All living things in an area plus the non-living things they interact with
Habitat
The natural home where an organism finds food, water, shelter, and space
Biotic factor
A living part of an ecosystem (plants, animals, bacteria, fungi)
Abiotic factor
A non-living part of an ecosystem (sunlight, water, soil, temperature, wind)
Producer
A living thing that makes its own food using sunlight (grass, trees, plankton)
Photosynthesis
The process by which producers use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make food
Consumer
A living thing that eats other living things for energy
Herbivore
A consumer that eats only plants (gazelle, goat, camel)
Carnivore
A consumer that eats only animals (lion, hyena)
Omnivore
A consumer that eats both plants and animals (human, chicken)
Primary consumer
Eats producers directly; the second trophic level
Secondary consumer
Eats primary consumers; the third trophic level

vocabulary.meaning: A consumer that eats only plants (gazelle, goat, camel)
vocabulary.example: A herbivore eats only plants — the gazelle, the goat, the cow, and the camel are herbivores.

vocabulary.meaning: A consumer that eats only animals (lion, hyena)
vocabulary.example: A carnivore eats only other animals — the lion, the hyena, and the fish-eating heron are carnivores.

vocabulary.meaning: A consumer that eats both plants and animals (human, chicken)
vocabulary.example: An omnivore eats both plants and animals — human beings are omnivores, and so are chickens and baboons.

vocabulary.meaning: Eats producers directly; the second trophic level
vocabulary.example: A primary consumer eats producers directly — it is a plant-eater, like the gazelle eating grass.

vocabulary.meaning: Eats primary consumers; the third trophic level
vocabulary.example: A secondary consumer eats primary consumers — like a snake eating a mouse, or a small fish eating tiny water animals.

commonMistakes: Drawing the food-chain arrow toward the food
The arrow shows energy flow, which goes into the eater, not the food
They recycle nutrients that producers need to grow
Believing energy stays the same up a chain
About ninety percent is lost at every step
Calling every animal a consumer of the same level
Animals sit at different trophic levels depending on what they eat
Thinking plastic will rot like a leaf
Plastic is not natural; decomposers cannot break it down for centuries

connections.text: Just as your digestive system gets energy from food, animals in a food chain pass energy along by eating.
Decomposition is a kind of change where materials break down — a bridge to studying how substances change.
Ecosystems link to the savanna, coast, and Rift Valley you study in geography, and to the dry and wet seasons.
Being a khalifah, a caretaker of the Earth, connects science to the value of protecting creation.
The ten percent energy rule uses division and percentages you practise in maths.
Observe a food chain near your home for a week and draw it accurately.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a producer and a consumer?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A producer makes its own food using sunlight (for example, grass), while a consumer cannot and must eat other living things (for example, a gazelle). Producers begin every food chain.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why the arrow in a food chain always points toward the animal that eats.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The arrow shows the direction that energy flows. Energy moves from the food into the animal that eats it, so the arrow points toward the eater. Grass -> gazelle, not the reverse.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name two decomposers and describe the job they do in an ecosystem.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Two decomposers are bacteria and fungi (earthworms and dung beetles are also acceptable). They break down dead plants, dead animals, and waste, returning nutrients to the soil for producers to reuse.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is only about ten percent of energy passed on at each step of a food chain?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: At each step, most energy is used up by the animal for living, moving, and breathing, and is lost as heat. Only about ten percent is stored in the body and available to the next animal.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give one adaptation of the camel and explain how it helps in dry, semi-arid land.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The camel stores fat in its hump for energy when food is scarce (other valid answers: long eyelashes against sand, wide feet, going days without water). This helps it survive long, dry periods.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A food chain shows one line of feeding relationships (grass -> gazelle -> lion). A food web joins many food chains together to show all the feeding links in an ecosystem, giving a truer picture.

rounds.explanation: acacia grass. Grass is a producer because it makes its own food by photosynthesis; the others must eat.

rounds.prompt: About how much energy passes from one level of a food chain to the next?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: 10 percent. About ninety percent is lost as heat and through living and moving, so only about ten percent passes on.

rounds.prompt: Why are there usually fewer lions than gazelles in a savanna?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: energy decreases up the chain. With little energy left at the top, only a few lions can be supported.

rounds.prompt: What would most likely happen if all decomposers disappeared?
choices: nutrients would return to the soil faster
dead matter would pile up and soil would grow poor
rounds.answer: dead matter would pile up and soil would grow poor
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: dead matter would pile up and the soil would grow poor. Nutrients would stay locked in dead things, so producers could not grow.

rounds.prompt: Which human activity harms ocean food webs by taking too many fish?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 2 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: overfishing. Catching fish faster than they can breed collapses fish populations and the ocean food web.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can explain what an ecosystem and a habitat are, and describe the biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) factors within them.
I can describe how plants act as producers and capture energy from the sun through photosynthesis.
I can classify animals as primary, secondary, and tertiary consumers, and as herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores.
I can explain the vital role of decomposers in recycling nutrients back into the soil.
I can build and read food chains and food webs, using arrows correctly to show the flow of energy.
I can explain why energy decreases at each step of a food chain and why there are fewer top predators than plants.
I can describe how living things show adaptations that help them survive in their habitat.
